justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple modes, including broad sidewalks, a bus stop on the left, and separated vehicle carriageways, which supports relatively equitable distribution of public space for all road users.

A central metal barrier organizes traffic streams and reduces vehicle conflicts, but it also makes mid-block crossing difficult and concentrates pedestrian crossing opportunities, which weakens fairness for people needing direct access across the boulevard.
Sidewalks on both sides appear continuous and fairly wide, indicating generally good physical accessibility for everyday movement, although no curb ramps or tactile paving are visible in this view.
The visible bus stop provides access for non-drivers, improving transport justice compared with a street designed only for private cars.
There is no clearly marked protected bicycle lane or bicycle-priority facility visible, so cycling users receive less dedicated space than motorists and pedestrians.
safety: The central median fence physically separates opposing traffic directions, lowering the risk of head-on conflicts and random pedestrian crossing into fast-moving lanes.
The roadway is wide, straight, and has clear lane markings, giving drivers strong sightlines and predictable movement patterns.
Streetlights are installed at regular intervals along the corridor, which suggests better nighttime visibility and general traffic safety.
The sidewalks are set back from moving traffic by curbs and planting strips in some sections, improving pedestrian protection from vehicles.
However, the long straight alignment may encourage higher vehicle speeds, which can reduce safety for crossing pedestrians and cyclists where formal crossings are sparse.
livability: Large mature street trees on both sides create a greener and more pleasant daily environment, supporting routine walking, waiting, and roadside activity.
A visible bus stop on the left adds practical mobility value and helps connect the street to daily destinations without requiring a car.
The street appears clean, orderly, and well maintained, with trimmed median planting and intact pavement, which supports everyday usability and perceived urban quality.
The corridor feels somewhat low in active frontage because there are few visible shops or transparent ground-floor uses directly engaging the sidewalk.
The broad sidewalks and shaded edges can support casual lingering, but there are no obvious benches or social seating features visible.
sustainability: Dense tree canopies along both sidewalks provide significant urban greenery, helping with shade, air quality improvement, and heat mitigation.
The presence of a bus stop supports public transport use and therefore a lower-carbon travel option than car-only streets.
The landscaped median and roadside vegetation indicate some investment in green infrastructure, even if no stormwater facilities are clearly visible.
The street design still dedicates a large amount of surface area to motor vehicle travel lanes, which reduces the overall sustainability balance.
No dedicated cycling lane is visible, limiting support for another important low-carbon mode.
aesthetics: The continuous rows of mature trees create a strong visual rhythm and give the boulevard an attractive, established character.
The street has a neat and coherent appearance, with uniform lamp posts, clean pavement, and a well-maintained planted median.
Open sky views and the long axial perspective produce a spacious and orderly boulevard image.
The greenery on both sides softens the hard roadway edges and significantly enhances visual appeal.
The corridor is visually pleasant but somewhat monotonous because of the long straight road and limited variation in building frontage.
comfort: Extensive tree canopy along both sidewalks likely provides meaningful shade for pedestrians and bus users, improving thermal comfort in sunny weather.
The sidewalks appear wide, even, and unobstructed in the visible sections, which supports comfortable walking and standing.
The planted median and roadside greenery can help buffer dust and improve the psychological comfort of the corridor.
There are no clearly visible benches or resting facilities near the sidewalks or bus stop, which limits physical comfort for waiting or longer stays.
Because the road is broad and designed for continuous vehicle movement, traffic noise and heat radiating from the asphalt may still reduce comfort near the carriageway.
walkability: Sidewalks are present on both sides of the boulevard and appear continuous, which is a basic strength for walkability.
Mature roadside trees provide shade and make walking more tolerable in daytime conditions.
The bus stop increases pedestrian relevance by generating walking access to transit.
The roadway is very wide and divided by fencing, and no marked pedestrian crossing is visible in the image, so crossing convenience appears limited.
The streetscape emphasizes through-movement rather than fine-grained pedestrian destinations, with little visible active frontage or seating to enrich the walking experience.
bikeability: No protected bike lane, painted bike lane, or clearly designated cycling space is visible on either side of the roadway.
The wide, straight carriageway may attract higher motor vehicle speeds, which makes on-road cycling feel less safe without dedicated protection.
The central barrier improves motor traffic order but does not provide any cycling-specific benefit and may complicate route flexibility for cyclists.
There are no visible bike parking racks, bike boxes, or bicycle wayfinding elements to support cycling convenience.
Although the corridor is spacious and visually open, the current design appears primarily car-oriented rather than bicycle-oriented.
